new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress falls on the penultimate syllable; the stressed syllable is usually realized with high pitch. The word 'generally' signals unstated exceptions. A second passage on p. 3 ('Conventions: Phonological') uses stress as a conditioning environment: 'The voiced plosives /b d g/ are prenasalized initially in stressed syllables. /b/ also weakens to [β] preceding /u/ in unstressed syllables.'
new_statements.exceptions: None listed; the statement is hedged with 'Generally' and 'usually' but no exceptions are named. No mention of vowel length or contrastive tone; the section heading covers tone, stress and length but only the stress sentence is filled
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD covers 'Duau (Duwau) language [DUA]' as a whole (Milne Bay, ~5000 speakers, Dobu-Duau network); it names no specific dialect. Its phonological note on /l/ ~ [r] ~ [ɾ] says 'There appears to be no correlation with dialect', so the description is meant to be pan-dialectal. The data derive from Leckie & Lithgow 1974 (Duwau phonemics).

audit.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim at p.3 of the OPD PDF we hold. The deciding source is a brief SIL phonology data sheet (2004, resting on a 1974 SIL phonemics Ms), hedged with 'generally', but it is first-hand and it is the only published phonological description of Duau in Glottolog, OLAC and SIL's own archive listing; no grammar, sketch, dissertation or instrumental study exists to supersede it. Held Lithgow 1976 §84 is silent on Duau specifically but its Papuan-Tip generalisations (Dobu penult lengthening; stress shifting rightward with suffixes) are consistent with a penultimate rule. Coding 'fixed penultimate, no weight/secondary stress described' matches the source; nothing found suggests it is wrong. Only improvement would be the unpublished 1974 Leckie & Lithgow Ms, access unknown.
